title: The Year of New Seeing
teaser: The razor slices the eye. In Kassel, Harald Szeemann canonizes conceptual art while John Berger teaches television viewers that seeing is never innocent. Deleuze and Guattari attack the Oedipal family; Calvino builds invisible cities. Nixon shakes Mao's hand. Black September murders Israeli athletes. Watergate's burglars fumble in the dark. The old ways of seeing — political, aesthetic, psychological — are all under assault.

art.label: Art
art.content: documenta 5 opens in Kassel under Harald Szeemann's radical curation, canonizing Conceptual Art and declaring that ideas matter more than objects. Joseph Beuys installs his Office for Direct Democracy; Gilbert & George present themselves as living sculptures; Daniel Buren wraps columns in stripes. Szeemann's concept of 'Individual Mythologies' liberates artists from movements entirely. Meanwhile, the BBC broadcasts John Berger's Ways of Seeing — four episodes that transform art criticism by exposing how images encode power, gender, and capital. Berger introduces the 'male gaze' and draws lines from Renaissance oil painting to modern advertising. At Cannes, Tarkovsky's Solaris wins the Grand Prix — science fiction as philosophical meditation on memory, love, and the limits of human understanding.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: Italo Calvino publishes Le città invisibili — Marco Polo describing fifty-five impossible cities to Kublai Khan, each a meditation on memory, desire, or death. Postmodern literature finds its purest expression: structure as meaning, cities as philosophical propositions. In Lisbon, three women — Maria Isabel Barreno, Maria Teresa Horta, and Maria Velho da Costa — publish Novas Cartas Portuguesas, a feminist collage that lands them in prison under the Estado Novo dictatorship. Their trial becomes an international cause, with Simone de Beauvoir and Doris Lessing demanding their release. In June, the Soviet Union expels Joseph Brodsky, who will become America's poet laureate — exile as the modern poet's condition.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari publish L'Anti-Œdipe, attacking Freud's Oedipal framework as capitalism's psychic enforcement mechanism. Desire, they argue, is not lack but production — the unconscious is a factory, not a theater. Their 'schizoanalysis' emerges from the failure of May 1968: if revolution failed, perhaps the revolutionary subject itself needs reimagining. Jacques Derrida's Marges de la philosophie extends deconstruction into the margins — footnotes, signatures, supplements — revealing that philosophy's apparent edges contain its hidden foundations. Post-structuralism consolidates its assault on stable meaning, stable subjects, stable anything.

hist.label: History
hist.content: On January thirtieth, British paratroopers kill fourteen unarmed civil rights marchers in Derry — Bloody Sunday ignites a generation of IRA recruitment and ensures the Troubles will last decades. On February twenty-first, Nixon lands in Beijing, shakes Mao's hand, and reshapes the Cold War's geometry. On June seventeenth, five burglars are caught in the Watergate complex — the beginning of the end for Nixon's presidency. On September fifth, Palestinian terrorists from Black September take Israeli athletes hostage at the Munich Olympics; the bungled rescue leaves eleven Israelis dead. The year draws lines in blood between peoples who will spend decades crossing them.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: The year's convergence is a crisis of ways of seeing — optical, political, psychological. Berger teaches that looking is ideological; Deleuze and Guattari argue that even desire is socially constructed; Szeemann demonstrates that art can be pure concept without object. Calvino's cities exist only in description — seeing them creates them. Meanwhile, the old geopolitical map tears: Nixon in China rewrites thirty years of Cold War assumptions; Black September brings Palestinian struggle to global television; Watergate reveals that American democracy's guardians were its burglars. The post-1968 question — why did revolution fail? — receives multiple answers: because we hadn't yet learned to see differently.
conn.funFact: Nixon's meeting with Mao lasted sixty-five minutes instead of the planned ten — the ailing Chairman insisted on talking, and no one dared interrupt.
